title: Al-Biruni: Measuring the Earth
summary: How the scholar Al-Biruni used a mountain, careful angle measurements, and mathematics to estimate the size of the Earth with remarkable accuracy about a thousand years ago.
poll: A single person with a clever idea can solve a problem that a large team cannot.

versions.title: The Man Who Sized Up the Earth
versions.text:
In 973, a boy was born in Central Asia. His name was Al-Biruni. He grew up to be a great scholar. He wrote more than 100 books.

He had a big question. How big is the Earth? Some men had tried to find out. They went a long way. The land was flat. They had to mark each step. It was hard work. It took lots of men. It took lots of time.

He had a new plan. He would use a mountain! First, he stood on flat land. He measured the angle to the top. That told him how tall it was.

Next, he went up to the top. He looked far out. Land and sky met in a line. That line is the horizon. It sat a bit low. He found that angle, too.

Then he did the math. It worked! Now he knew how big the Earth was! His plan took just one man and one hill.

How close was he? He said the Earth's center was down 6,340 kilometers. Today we say 6,371. That is very close!

He did this at a fort. It is in what is now Pakistan. Now a crater on the moon has his name.

versions.title: Al-Biruni: Measuring the Earth
versions.text:
In 973, a boy named Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia. Today it is part of Uzbekistan. He grew up to become a great scholar. He studied the stars, math, maps, and history, and he wrote more than 100 works.

One question interested him a lot: How large is the Earth? Earlier scholars had tried to answer it by walking across flat land and measuring a very long distance. Their method worked, but it needed many people and a great deal of time.

Al-Biruni found a simpler way that used a mountain. First, he stood on the flat plain near the mountain. He measured the angle from the ground to its peak. This angle helped him work out how tall the mountain was.

Next, he climbed to the top and looked toward the horizon, where the land seems to meet the sky. Because the Earth is round, the horizon looked a little lower than a flat line. He measured this small angle, too. It was so small that he had to be very careful.

Finally, he used math to put his numbers together. He worked out the radius of the Earth, which is the distance from its center to its surface. His method needed only one person, one mountain, and good tools.

His answer was about 6,340 kilometers. Today, scientists say the average radius is about 6,371 kilometers. His answer was very accurate. It was off by less than one percent.

Al-Biruni believed that ideas should be tested by careful checking. He made these measurements at a fort in what is now Pakistan. Today, a crater on the moon is named for him.

versions.title: Al-Biruni: The Scholar Who Measured the Earth
versions.text:
In 973, a boy named Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia that is now part of Uzbekistan. He grew up to become a remarkable scholar who investigated astronomy, mathematics, geography, and history, and during his long life he produced more than 100 works, including a famous study of India for which he learned the Sanskrit language.

One question particularly fascinated him: How large is the Earth? Earlier scholars had attempted to answer it by traveling across flat land and measuring an extremely long distance, then comparing the positions of stars at each end. Their method was valuable, but it required numerous people and a considerable amount of time.

Al-Biruni developed a simpler approach that relied on a mountain. First, standing on the flat plain near the mountain, he used an astrolabe to measure the angle from the ground to its peak. With trigonometry, the mathematics of triangles, this angle allowed him to calculate the mountain's height.

Next, he climbed to the summit and gazed toward the horizon, where the land appears to meet the sky. Because the Earth is curved, the horizon appeared slightly below a perfectly level line, so he carefully measured this small angle as well. The angle was tiny, only a little more than half a degree, so even a slight error would have changed his result considerably.

Finally, he combined his measurements in a single calculation to estimate the radius of the Earth, which is the distance from its center to its surface. His method required only one person, one mountain, and careful observation.

His answer was approximately 6,340 kilometers. Today, scientists calculate the average radius as approximately 6,371 kilometers, which means his estimate was off by less than one percent.

Al-Biruni believed that knowledge should be tested by careful observation rather than simply accepted from earlier authorities, and he frequently repeated his measurements to confirm them. He conducted these measurements at a fort in what is now Pakistan. Today, a crater on the moon is named in his honor.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare Al-Biruni's estimate with the modern value of 6,371 kilometers?
options: To show that modern scientists copied him
To show how remarkably accurate his method was
To prove that the Earth has shrunk since his time
To argue that his method was a failure
questions.why: Comparing his 6,340 kilometers with 6,371 shows his estimate differed by less than one percent.

wrong.A: The article does not claim modern scientists copied him.
wrong.C: The difference reflects measurement, not a shrinking Earth.
wrong.D: The comparison shows success, not failure.

questions.stem: In the article, the word estimate most nearly means —
options: a careful calculation that may not be exact
a wild guess with no evidence
a perfect measurement with no error at all
a type of mountain found in Pakistan
questions.why: His estimate was a careful calculation based on measurements, close but not exactly equal to the modern value.

wrong.B: His estimate was based on evidence and math.
wrong.C: His result was close, but not perfect.

questions.stem: How does Al-Biruni's method differ from the earlier scholars' method?
options: Both needed large teams traveling for months.
His worked from one place; theirs needed long journeys.
Theirs used a mountain, while his used flat land.
Neither used the positions of stars or angles.
questions.why: Earlier scholars traveled across flat land measuring long distances; Al-Biruni worked from one mountain.

wrong.A: Only the earlier method needed many people and much time.
wrong.C: It is the reverse: he used a mountain, and they used flat land.
wrong.D: Earlier scholars compared star positions, and Al-Biruni measured angles.

HIGH.prompt: Al-Biruni believed knowledge should be tested by careful observation. Explain how his measurement of the Earth shows this belief, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained his belief in my own words.
I connected the belief to at least two parts of his method.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
